metric.why: Idle servers burn power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing. Fleet utilization is where the money hides in most enterprise estates, and it is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest.
metric.definition: The share of provisioned compute doing real work, measured over time rather than at peak.

reading.body:
Server utilization rate—the share of provisioned compute actually doing work—is the denominator that makes every efficiency metric honest, because idle infrastructure burns power, licenses, and depreciation while producing nothing.

Most enterprise data centers run far below peak capacity most of the time. The gap between provisioned servers and utilized servers is where the money hides. This gap matters to AI infrastructure specifically because AI workloads are often bursty and unpredictable, forcing operators to overprovision to meet peak demand. If utilization stays low across the fleet, the building and power cost per unit of actual compute rises, and the economic case for scaling deteriorates.

Measuring utilization over time rather than at peak is what reveals the real picture. A data center that hits 80 percent utilization at 3 a.m. on Tuesday looks different from one that sustains 80 percent across the week. The time-averaged number tells you whether your power subscription and building footprint are actually earning their keep, or whether you have stranded capacity that the grid could use elsewhere.

This metric does not tell you whether the work being done is valuable, whether the power is renewable, or whether the building itself has hit its physical limits. It only shows how much of what you built is in use.
